subject: Banking
title: Dark Pools
description: A quick, practical guide to Dark Pools.

hook.text: A giant sell order on a public exchange can move the price before the first share even trades.

buildup.text: If a pension fund puts a 5-million-share sell order on a public exchange, the price would crash before the order fills.

discovery.text: Dark pools match large orders anonymously. The trade happens at market price without alerting other traders.

twist.text: Dark pools now handle about 40% of all US stock trading. The majority of volume happens where you cannot see it.

climax.text: Dark pools protect large traders but reduce market transparency.

punchline.text: 40% of US stock trading is invisible. Dark pools hide real volume.

quiz.question: Why do institutional investors use dark pools?
options: To execute large trades without moving the market price against them

details.summary: Dark pools are private trading venues where large institutional investors buy and sell securities anonymously, away from public exchanges, to avoid moving market prices with their massive order sizes.
details.whyItMatters: Dark pools now handle nearly 40 percent of US stock trading volume. Their opacity raises concerns about fairness because regular investors cannot see the prices and volumes being traded in these private markets.
takeaways: Institutional investors use dark pools to hide large orders from the market
Nearly 40 percent of US stock trading occurs in dark pools
Regulators worry about reduced transparency and price discovery

faq.question: Why do institutional investors need dark pools?
faq.answer: A pension fund selling a million shares on a public exchange would crash the price as traders front-run the order. Dark pools let them execute large trades without revealing their intentions, getting better prices for their beneficiaries.

faq.question: Are dark pools legal?
faq.answer: Yes. They are regulated by the SEC and must report trades after execution. However, several dark pool operators have been fined for giving preferential access to high-frequency traders, undermining the anonymity they promise.
